answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1838–1914 · Scottish-American naturalist & father of the U.S. national parks
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed. Muir wrote it in a letter to his sister Sarah Muir Galloway from Yosemite Valley on 3 September 1873; the holograph survives at the University of the Pacific ↗ and it was printed in The Life and Letters of John Muir (1923). The catch: the famous line is only the first half of Muir’s sentence.

source.excerpt: The mountains are calling and I must go, and I will work on while I can, studying incessantly.
trail: The Sierra Club’s John Muir Exhibit ↗ prints the line from a “letter to sister Sarah Galloway, September 3, 1873,” and flags that it is usually quoted only in part.
The University of the Pacific ↗, which holds the original manuscript, confirms the holograph reads “The mountains are calling and I must go and I will work on while I can, studying incessantly.”
It first reached print in William Frederic Badé’s The Life and Letters of John Muir, ch. 10 ↗ (Houghton Mifflin, 1923).
source.excerptNote: The famous version stops at “must go.” Muir’s sentence keeps going — the calling was to relentless work and study, not just to wander.

source.rightsNote: Muir wrote the letter in 1873; it was first published in The Life and Letters of John Muir (1923). Both the writing and its first publication predate 1931, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.metaLine: 1838–1914 · Naturalist, writer & father of the U.S. national parks
author.bio: John Muir (1838–1914) was a Scottish-born American naturalist, glaciologist and writer whose lyrical accounts of the Sierra Nevada helped establish Yosemite and other national parks. He co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892 and served as its first president, becoming the most influential voice of early American conservation.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets misquoted
misattribution.intro: The words really are Muir’s — the trouble is what posters and mugs leave off.

items.why: Muir’s full sentence runs “…and I must go, and I will work on while I can, studying incessantly.” Dropping the second half turns a line about relentless work and study ↗ into a pure call of the wild.
Popular versions often insert a comma (“The mountains are calling, and I must go”) and an exclamation point that Muir’s manuscript letter ↗ does not contain.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely John Muir — a verbatim clause from an 1873 letter to his sister ↗, routinely quoted at half length.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Muir wrote the line at 35, just back from a punishing five-week solo expedition among the High Sierra glaciers. Far from a tourist’s daydream, it was a report to his sister on why he could not settle to a desk: the peaks pulled him back, but so did an obsessive program of measurement and study that would help make the case for saving Yosemite.
Read whole, the sentence captures the two halves of Muir’s life — wonder and work — that would soon feed the campaign for national parks and the founding of the Sierra Club.
context.pull: The calling was to work and study — not just to wander.
